name: Toxicology & Environmental
sub: Antidotes, toxidromes, overdose, poisoning, heat and cold

cards.q: What is the antidote and dose for paracetamol poisoning?
cards.a: N-acetylcysteine: 150 mg/kg over 1 h, 50 mg/kg over 4 h, 100 mg/kg over 16 h. Use the Rumack–Matthew nomogram after a single acute ingestion (4 h level).

cards.q: Describe the cholinergic toxidrome and antidotes.
cards.a: DUMBELS/SLUDGE: diarrhoea, urination, miosis, bradycardia, bronchorrhoea, emesis, lacrimation, salivation. Give atropine 2–5 mg IV repeated until secretions dry, and pralidoxime for organophosphates.

cards.q: What is the antidote for opioid overdose and dosing?
cards.a: Naloxone 0.4–2 mg IV/IM/IN, repeat every 2–3 min; infusion at two-thirds of the effective dose per hour because of its short half-life.

cards.q: How do you treat benzodiazepine overdose?
cards.a: Supportive airway and ventilation. Flumazenil is generally avoided because it can precipitate seizures in dependent patients or mixed ingestions.

cards.q: What are the ECG and treatment features of tricyclic antidepressant overdose?
cards.a: QRS >100 ms, terminal R in aVR, tachycardia, hypotension, seizures. Give sodium bicarbonate 1–2 mmol/kg until QRS narrows, target pH 7.45–7.55, and treat seizures with benzodiazepines.

cards.q: What is the treatment of calcium-channel blocker or beta-blocker overdose?
cards.a: Calcium, high-dose insulin euglycaemia therapy (1 unit/kg bolus then 0.5–1 unit/kg/h with dextrose), vasopressors, glucagon (beta-blockers), and lipid emulsion or ECMO in refractory shock.

cards.q: What are the symptoms and treatment of digoxin toxicity?
cards.a: Nausea, visual disturbance, bradyarrhythmias, hyperkalaemia, ventricular ectopy. Give digoxin-specific Fab (about 10 vials for acute ingestion if unstable) and correct potassium and magnesium.

cards.q: How do you treat toxic alcohol (methanol/ethylene glycol) poisoning?
cards.a: Fomepizole 15 mg/kg IV then 10 mg/kg every 12 h (or ethanol), correct acidosis, thiamine/folate/pyridoxine, and haemodialysis for severe acidosis (pH <7.25), visual symptoms or renal failure.

cards.q: What is the management of cyanide poisoning?
cards.a: 100% oxygen, hydroxocobalamin 5 g IV over 15 minutes (second dose if needed), sodium thiosulphate, and supportive care.

cards.q: How is carbon monoxide poisoning treated?
cards.a: 100% oxygen via non-rebreather or ventilator to shorten the half-life; consider hyperbaric oxygen for loss of consciousness, neurological signs, pregnancy or COHb >25%. Pulse oximetry is unreliable.

cards.q: What is the serotonin syndrome triad and treatment?
cards.a: Mental status change, autonomic instability and neuromuscular excitation (clonus, hyperreflexia). Stop agents, benzodiazepines, cyproheptadine, cooling and paralysis for severe hyperthermia.

cards.q: How does neuroleptic malignant syndrome differ from serotonin syndrome?
cards.a: NMS develops over days with bradyreflexia and lead-pipe rigidity after dopamine antagonists; treat with stopping the drug, cooling, dantrolene or bromocriptine.

cards.q: What is the treatment for malignant hyperthermia?
cards.a: Stop triggering agents (volatile anaesthetics, suxamethonium), hyperventilate with 100% oxygen, give dantrolene 2.5 mg/kg IV (repeat to 10 mg/kg), cool, and correct hyperkalaemia.

cards.q: How do you manage salicylate poisoning?
cards.a: Alkalinise urine with sodium bicarbonate (urine pH 7.5–8.0), maintain potassium, avoid intubation unless necessary (and match minute ventilation), and haemodialysis for severe toxicity.

cards.q: What is the antidote for iron overdose?
cards.a: Deferoxamine 15 mg/kg/h IV for symptomatic patients or serum iron >500 µg/dL (90 µmol/L).

cards.q: What is the management of methaemoglobinaemia from dapsone or nitrites?
cards.a: Methylene blue 1–2 mg/kg IV over 5 minutes; repeat if needed; avoid in G6PD deficiency.

cards.q: How is lithium toxicity treated?
cards.a: Isotonic saline, avoid nephrotoxins, and haemodialysis for severe neurotoxicity, renal failure or levels >4 mmol/L (or >2.5 with symptoms).

cards.q: What is the management of heat stroke?
cards.a: Rapid active cooling (cold-water immersion or evaporative methods) to <39 °C within 30 minutes, fluid resuscitation, and supportive care for organ failure; antipyretics are ineffective.

cards.q: How is severe hypothermia managed?
cards.a: Gentle handling, warm IV fluids, active internal rewarming (e.g. bladder lavage, ECMO) for temperatures <28–30 °C or arrest, and continued CPR until rewarmed ('not dead until warm and dead').

cards.q: What is the treatment of snake envenomation with coagulopathy?
cards.a: Early polyvalent antivenom (initial 10 vials in neurotoxic or haemotoxic envenomation), 20-minute whole blood clotting test, supportive care, and avoid tourniquets and incisions.

cards.q: A drowsy patient has pinpoint pupils and RR 6/min. What is the first-line treatment?
cards.e: Miosis and respiratory depression indicate opioid toxicity: ventilate and give titrated naloxone.

cards.q: A patient has a wide QRS of 140 ms after amitriptyline overdose. What is the best drug?
cards.e: Sodium loading and alkalinisation counteract fast sodium channel blockade from TCAs; class I and III antiarrhythmics worsen toxicity.
